summary: Proposes the Media Delivery Index (MDI), a measurement for diagnosing or rating networks that carry streaming media, video, voice over IP, or other traffic sensitive to timing and loss. It indicates jitter, deviation from nominal flow rates, and data loss at a glance. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A score that tells you how smoothly a video stream is flowing, like a gauge for whether your water hose is steady or sputtering.

questions: how to measure jitter for video streams
subtitle: Measures network jitter and loss for streaming media delivery.

tldr.problem: Networks carrying streaming media like video need a simple way to detect jitter and packet loss that affect quality. Diagnosing where problems occur in complex networks with multiple QoS methods is difficult.
tldr.mechanism: The Media Delivery Index (MDI) combines two measurements: the Delay Factor (maximum buffer needed due to jitter) and the Media Loss Rate (count of lost or out-of-order packets). The result DF:MLR provides a quick indicator of streaming performance.
tldr.outcome: MDI lets network operators and switches quickly identify where jitter or loss is occurring in a stream, making troubleshooting easier for IPTV and other real-time applications.

facts.label: Measurement interval
facts.value: 1 second (typical for streams 1 Mb/s and higher)

facts.label: Suitable for
facts.value: MPEG transport stream, voice over IP, and other time-sensitive UDP applications

today: RFC 4445 is Informational and remains unchanged since April 2006. It provides a vendor-neutral approach to measuring streaming media quality. The measurements it defines suit modern IPTV deployments and streaming applications, though the RFC notes that other IETF standards (RFCs 3393 and 3611) offer complementary metrics.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Large networks now carry streaming media such as MPEG video, requiring both constant bandwidth and protection from packet loss. Methods like RSVP and Diffserv provide Quality of Service (QoS), but networks need a simple way to measure and diagnose real-time streaming performance. The MDI provides a targeted, efficient metric focused on the two key impairments: jitter and loss.

While earlier approaches like RTCP extended reports and IP packet delay variation metrics exist, the MDI is designed to be economical to compute and scalable for monitoring large numbers of streams in production networks, especially for IPTV deployments.
sections.eli5: When you watch a video, two things can go wrong: the picture stutters (jitter) or parts disappear (loss). The MDI measures both problems so you can fix them.

sections.title: How MDI Works
sections.content: The MDI combines two components. The Delay Factor (DF) measures the maximum difference between the rate packets arrive and the rate they should be consumed (the nominal drain rate). It tells you the minimum buffer size needed at a receiver to prevent underflow or overflow. The DF is expressed in milliseconds and updated every measurement interval, typically 1 second. The Media Loss Rate (MLR) counts lost or out-of-order packets during the same interval. When multiple streaming packets fit in one IP packet (for example, seven 188-byte MPEG transport stream packets in an IP packet), an IP packet loss counts as multiple lost packets.
sections.eli5: The Delay Factor is like a water level gauge: it shows how high the buffer fills when packets bunch up. The Media Loss Rate is a counter that counts dropped packages. Together they tell you if your stream is in trouble.

sections.title: Computing the Delay Factor
sections.content: The DF calculation uses a virtual buffer model. As each packet arrives during a measurement interval, compute the buffer state just before and just after the arrival. The buffer size is the running sum of packet sizes minus the data consumed at the nominal media rate up to that point. After processing all packets in an interval, the DF equals the maximum buffer minus the minimum buffer, divided by the media rate. For a 3.75 Mb/s MPEG transport stream, a DF of 50 milliseconds means the buffer must hold at least 50 milliseconds worth of that stream to prevent loss. The measurement interval should be long enough to capture network behavior; 1 second is recommended for streams of 1 Mb/s and higher.
sections.eli5: Imagine pouring water into a bucket at a changing rate while draining it at a steady rate. The DF measures the largest difference between how full the bucket gets and how empty it gets. That tells you the minimum bucket size you need.

sections.title: Practical Use of MDI
sections.content: By monitoring MDI at multiple points in a network, operators can quickly identify which device or link introduces jitter or loss. A high DF suggests packet bunching or gaps caused by buffering in intermediate switches. A rising DF over time indicates growing network congestion. A high MLR directly shows packet loss. Different decoders tolerate different DF and MLR values; characterizing a decoder's maximum acceptable MDI helps set network provisioning targets. MDI can be computed at modest cost using switch CPU for small numbers of flows or dedicated hardware for all flows on a link.
sections.eli5: By testing the stream at different points in the network, you can pinpoint where the jitter or loss starts. If the buffer fills more and more, congestion is coming. If packets disappear, something on the path is dropping them.

sections.title: When to Use MDI
sections.content: MDI is most useful for monitoring constant bit rate streams like MPEG video and voice over IP over UDP. The RFC notes that variable bit rate streams are more complex but possible if the stream's dynamic drain rate can be determined. The measurement works because it requires only access to packet payload headers (like MPEG transport stream headers) to determine sequence numbers and nominal rates; encrypted content does not affect the measurement. MDI suits production networks with many streams, particularly IPTV services, where per-stream monitoring can quickly isolate performance problems.
sections.eli5: MDI works best for steady video streams. If you know how fast the data should flow out, you can measure if packets are getting stuck or lost. You don't need to see the actual video to check the stream's health.

items.title: Delay Factor
items.text: Maximum difference between packet arrival rate and drain rate, expressed in milliseconds. Indicates required buffer size.

items.title: Media Loss Rate
items.text: Count of lost or out-of-order packets per measurement interval. Directly measures data loss.
